Greek & Mediterranean Pantry Essentials: What I Always Keep on Hand

Basics

Sharing is caring!

Greek & Mediterranean Pantry Essentials: What I Always Keep on Hand

Instaread

If you have ever opened your pantry at 5 p.m. and wondered what in the world to make for dinner, this guide is for you.

You do not need an overflowing pantry or dozens of specialty ingredients to cook delicious Greek and Mediterranean food. Most of my recipes begin with the same dependable staples: good olive oil, lemons, garlic, oregano, tomatoes, beans, rice, pasta, and a few bold ingredients that make everything taste special.

That is one of the things I love most about this way of cooking. The ingredients are simple, economical, and meant to be used in many different ways.

A can of tomatoes can become soup, sauce, or youvetsi. A bag of lentils can feed the family for very little. Lemons, olive oil, garlic, and oregano can transform potatoes, chicken, fish, vegetables, or beans.

This is not a list of everything you could possibly buy. These are the Greek and Mediterranean pantry essentials I actually reach for in my kitchen—the ingredients that help me get a delicious meal on the table without making cooking complicated or expensive.

Short on Time? Start With These 12 Essentials

If you are stocking your pantry from scratch, please do not feel as though you need to buy everything on this page at once.

Begin with these twelve ingredients:

  1. Extra-virgin olive oil
  2. Greek oregano
  3. Kosher salt or sea salt
  4. Black peppercorns
  5. Fresh garlic
  6. Yellow onions
  7. Fresh lemons
  8. Canned tomatoes
  9. Tomato paste
  10. Chickpeas or white beans
  11. Rice or orzo
  12. Chicken or vegetable broth

With these twelve ingredients—and a protein or vegetable—you can make dozens of simple meals.

Start here. Then add the remaining staples gradually as you cook your way through my recipes and discover what your family enjoys most.

The Mediterranean Flavor Foundation

These are the ingredients that do the most work in my kitchen. They are the foundation of so many Greek and Mediterranean recipes.

Extra-Virgin Olive Oil

Olive oil is more than a cooking fat in Greek cuisine. It is one of the main flavors.

I use extra-virgin olive oil for sautéing, roasting, dressings, marinades, soups, sauces, dips, and finishing dishes at the table. Sometimes all warm bread needs is good olive oil, herbs, and a little salt.

Choose an extra-virgin olive oil that tastes good to you. For everyday cooking, I prefer one with a fresh, balanced flavor that is not overwhelmingly bitter.

Keep olive oil away from heat and direct sunlight. A dark bottle or tin helps protect it, but I still would not store it directly beside the stove.

Use it in my Mediterranean Dips and Bread Dipping Oils or these reader-favorite Greek Lemony Roasted Potatoes.

Fresh Lemons and Red Wine Vinegar

Mediterranean food needs acidity. It wakes up the other flavors and keeps rich dishes from feeling heavy.

I use fresh lemon juice in marinades, soups, roasted potatoes, tahini sauce, beans, chicken, fish, and salad dressings. Red wine vinegar gives salads, braised dishes, beans, and marinades a deeper tang.

Before juicing a lemon, zest it. Freeze the zest and juice separately in small portions so none of that flavor goes to waste.

Fresh Garlic and Yellow Onions

Garlic and onions form the savory beginning of countless meals.

I use fresh garlic when it is an important flavor in a sauce, dip, marinade, or dressing. Yellow onions are my everyday choice because they work in soups, braises, meatballs, sauces, rice dishes, and roasted vegetables.

I also keep granulated garlic and onion powder in the pantry. They are not replacements for fresh garlic and onion in every recipe, but they are very useful in dry seasoning blends, meat mixtures, roasted vegetables, and quick weeknight meals.

The Herbs and Spices I Use Most

You do not need an enormous spice collection to cook my recipes. These are the seasonings I use again and again.

Greek Oregano

If you buy only one Greek herb, make it oregano.

I use it in marinades, lemon potatoes, salads, meatballs, chicken, vegetables, beans, sauces, and bread dipping oils. Greek oregano tends to have a strong, earthy flavor, so a little can go a long way.

Dried Dill

Dried dill is especially useful in soups, beans, spinach dishes, potatoes, sauces, and savory pies. I love fresh dill too, but dried dill means I can still add that familiar flavor when there is no fresh dill in the refrigerator.

Dried Thyme

Thyme adds a warm, earthy note to chicken, vegetables, beans, soups, and tomato-based dishes.

Bay Leaves

Add a bay leaf to simmering beans, lentils, soups, broth, or tomato sauce. It creates a subtle background flavor that makes the finished dish taste more complete.

Always remove the leaf before serving.

Ground Cumin and Coriander

These warm, savory spices are useful for meatballs, legumes, marinades, soups, and roasted vegetables. Ground coriander has a mild citrusy quality that works beautifully with cumin, garlic, lemon, and paprika.

Sweet Paprika

Sweet paprika adds beautiful color and gentle sweetness without making a dish spicy. I use it in meat mixtures, chicken dishes, soups, roasted vegetables, and marinades.

Cinnamon, Nutmeg, and Cloves

These spices are not only for baking.

A little cinnamon can add warmth to a Greek meat sauce. Nutmeg is wonderful in béchamel, creamy sauces, savory pies, and holiday baking. Cloves add deep warmth to syrups, braised dishes, and desserts.

The key is to use them lightly. They should support the other flavors without taking over.

Crushed Red Pepper and Sumac

Crushed red pepper adds quick heat to pasta, soup, roasted vegetables, and sauces.

Sumac is bright, tangy, and almost lemony. Sprinkle it over salads, onions, chicken, roasted vegetables, dips, or yogurt sauces.

Granulated Garlic and Onion Powder

I always keep both on hand. They are convenient when fresh garlic and onion are not practical, and they distribute evenly through meatballs, seasoning blends, breading, and roasted vegetables.

Buy smaller spice containers unless you use something constantly. The best value is the spice you finish while it is still fragrant—not the giant container that sits in the cabinet for five years.

Tomatoes and Tomato Paste

Canned tomatoes are among the hardest-working ingredients in my pantry.

I keep whole peeled tomatoes, crushed tomatoes, or both. They become pasta sauce, soup, braised vegetables, casseroles, and comforting baked dishes.

Tomato paste adds concentrated flavor and helps a quick sauce taste as if it has cooked much longer.

If a recipe uses only one or two tablespoons of tomato paste, freeze the remainder in tablespoon-sized portions. Once frozen, transfer the portions to a freezer bag. The next time a recipe needs a little tomato paste, it is already measured.

Put those tomatoes to work in my Keftedes Youvetsi: One-Pan Baked Meatballs and Orzo or Mediterranean Dirty Cabbage with Beef.

Beans, Lentils, and Yellow Split Peas

Legumes are some of the most economical and versatile foods you can keep in your kitchen.

I stock:

  • Chickpeas
  • White beans
  • Brown or green lentils
  • Yellow split peas

Canned beans are perfect for quick meals. Dried beans are wonderful when you have time and usually offer the best value. I use both.

Unless a recipe specifically tells you to use the liquid, rinse canned beans before adding them to a dish.

Chickpeas can become dips, soups, salads, grain bowls, or a quick meal with tomatoes, cucumbers, feta, and olives.

White beans are delicious in soups, tomato-based dishes, salads, and simple sautés with garlic, greens, and lemon.

Lentils cook relatively quickly and do not require soaking. They are perfect for inexpensive, comforting soups.

Try my classic Greek Lentil Soup, or Fakes, Lentil Soup with Spinach and Feta, or Creamy Vegan Fasolada with White Beans and Kale.

Rice, Orzo, Bucatini, Couscous, and Pasta

You do not need every grain and pasta shape at the grocery store. A small, useful selection will give you plenty of variety.

Long-Grain Rice

I use long-grain rice in pilafs, soups, stuffed vegetables, chicken dishes, and simple side dishes.

Rice can also stretch a small amount of meat or vegetables into a complete family meal.

Orzo

Orzo belongs in every Greek pantry.

Use it in soups, salads, side dishes, and baked meals such as youvetsi. Because it cooks like pasta but feels a little like rice, it is one of those ingredients that can go in many different directions.

Make my Keftedes Youvetsi when you want a comforting one-pan dinner.

Bucatini

Bucatini is one of my favorite pastas for hearty sauces. It looks similar to thick spaghetti, but the hollow center catches even more sauce.

Use it with a rich tomato sauce, meat sauce, or a simple pantry sauce made with tomatoes, garlic, olives, and capers.

Couscous

Couscous cooks very quickly, making it a helpful base for roasted vegetables, chicken, chickpeas, feta, and herbs.

Everyday Short Pasta

Keep one short pasta shape you know your family enjoys. It can become soup, pasta salad, a baked casserole, or a quick pantry dinner.

For more family-friendly ideas, visit my collection of 15 Easy Mediterranean Chicken Recipes for Busy Weeknights.

Breadcrumbs and Broth

Unseasoned breadcrumbs or panko can bind meatballs, add crunch to baked dishes, and create a quick topping for pasta or roasted vegetables.

I prefer unseasoned breadcrumbs because they allow me to control the herbs, salt, and spices.

Use them in my Greek Keftedes, then serve the meatballs with Creamy Tahini Sauce.

Broth turns pantry ingredients into soup, pilaf, sauce, or a braised dish with very little effort. I keep chicken broth and vegetable broth on hand so I have options for different recipes.

Choose a lower-sodium broth when possible. You can always add salt, but you cannot easily remove it.

My Bold-Flavor Shelf

You do not need to purchase all these ingredients immediately. Choose two or three you already enjoy, then add the others when you have a recipe planned.

Kalamata Olives

Kalamata olives add salty richness to salads, chicken, pasta, bread, grain bowls, and mezze platters.

Capers

A spoonful of capers can wake up fish, tomato sauce, pasta, roasted vegetables, and salads.

Jarred Grape Leaves

Jarred grape leaves keep well and allow you to make dolmades without having to find fresh grape leaves.

Once opened, follow the storage instructions on the jar and keep the remaining leaves covered in their brine.

Jarred Harissa

Harissa adds deep chile flavor to marinades, soups, roasted vegetables, eggs, and sauces.

Different brands vary significantly in heat, so begin with a small amount. You can always add more.

Roasted Red Peppers

Jarred roasted peppers can be blended into dips or added to eggs, sandwiches, pasta, grain bowls, salads, and chicken dishes.

Sun-Dried Tomatoes

Sun-dried tomatoes add concentrated tomato flavor to pasta, chicken, eggs, dips, savory bakes, and salads.

Canned Artichoke Hearts

Canned or jarred artichoke hearts are an easy shortcut for pasta, dips, casseroles, eggs, and savory pies.

Use them in my Artichoke Phyllo Tart.

Tahini

Tahini is sesame paste, and it is the base of so many creamy Mediterranean and Middle Eastern sauces, dressings, dips, and sweets.

The oil can separate while the jar sits. Stir it very well before measuring.

If the tahini at the bottom has become difficult to mix, transfer the contents to a food processor or blender and blend until smooth.

Make my Creamy Tahini Sauce and serve it with meatballs, roasted vegetables, chicken, pita, or grain bowls.

Honey

Honey is useful for breakfast, marinades, salad dressings, cheese boards, tea, and Greek desserts.

Red Wine Vinegar

Red wine vinegar is the natural partner to olive oil in Greek salad dressings and marinades. It also balances rich beans, meats, and braised dishes.

What I Keep in the Refrigerator

My refrigerator staples finish many of the dishes that begin in the pantry.

Feta in Brine

I prefer feta sold in brine because it usually has better flavor and texture and stays fresh longer.

Crumble it over salads, beans, eggs, vegetables, pasta, potatoes, and soup. Keep the remaining feta submerged in its brine in the refrigerator.

Plain Greek Yogurt

Greek yogurt can become breakfast, a marinade, a creamy dressing, a quick dip, or a cooling sauce for spicy food.

Eggs

Eggs are one of the easiest ways to turn leftover vegetables, grains, or potatoes into a meal.

Butter

Olive oil is my everyday cooking fat, but I keep butter for baking and for dishes that need its richness.

Parmesan or Kefalotiri

A flavorful hard cheese finishes pasta, gratins, savory pies, soups, roasted vegetables, and baked dishes beautifully.

Fresh Parsley and Dill

Fresh and dried herbs are both useful, but they do different jobs.

Dried herbs can simmer with a dish and build flavor. Fresh parsley and dill add color and freshness at the end.

Carrots and Celery

Carrots, celery, and onions are the quiet beginning of countless soups, sauces, and braised dishes.

Cucumbers and Tomatoes

Add feta, Kalamata olives, olive oil, oregano, and bread, and you already have the beginnings of a beautiful lunch.

What I Keep in the Freezer

The freezer is my backup pantry. These are the ingredients that rescue busy nights and help me waste less food:

  • Phyllo dough
  • Puff pastry
  • Frozen spinach
  • Peas
  • Green beans
  • Artichoke hearts
  • Pearl onions
  • Frozen chopped garlic
  • Pita bread
  • Nuts
  • Portioned tomato paste
  • Lemon juice and zest
  • Cooked beans
  • Homemade broth

Freeze nuts in airtight bags so they stay fresh longer.

Thaw phyllo in the refrigerator, keep it well wrapped, and follow the package directions. Once you begin working with it, cover the unused sheets so they do not dry out.

Frozen chopped garlic is very convenient when you need to get dinner started quickly. I still use fresh garlic when garlic is one of the main flavors in a recipe.

Use your freezer staples to make my Artichoke Phyllo Tart, Greek-Style Pita Chips, or Saragli Baklava Pinwheels.

Mix, Match, and Make Dinner

Dinner does not always need to begin with a new recipe or another trip to the grocery store.

Use this simple formula:

Choose one base + one flavor direction + one fresh finish.

You can also use these easy combinations without following a formal recipe:

  • Rice + chickpeas + roasted peppers + feta + lemon
  • Bucatini + canned tomatoes + capers + olives
  • White beans + broth + chopped garlic + dill + lemon
  • Eggs + frozen spinach + feta + oregano
  • Orzo + broth + frozen spinach + Parmesan or kefalotiri
  • Pita + tahini sauce + cucumbers + tomatoes + olives

Before serving, taste the food.

Many simple Mediterranean dishes need one of four things at the end: a pinch of salt, a squeeze of lemon, a drizzle of olive oil, or a handful of fresh herbs.

That final adjustment can make the entire dish come alive.

How to Stock Your Pantry Without Overspending

Shop your kitchen first

Check your pantry, refrigerator, and freezer before making a shopping list. You may already own more of these ingredients than you realize.

Begin with the core twelve

You do not need every spice, pasta shape, and specialty jar immediately. Buy the foundation first.

Choose ingredients that work in several meals

Feta, for example, can finish salads, eggs, soup, pasta, roasted vegetables, beans, and savory pies.

Keep one dependable option in each category

One rice, one short pasta, one orzo, one canned bean, and one good broth are enough to begin.

You can add variety when you know you will use it.

Label and date freezer items

This is especially helpful for broth, cooked beans, lemon juice, zest, tomato paste, and nuts.

Plan around opened ingredients

If you open roasted red peppers for pasta, use the remainder in eggs, sandwiches, a dip, or a grain bowl that week.

If you open feta for a salad, use it the next day with eggs or crumble it over soup.

Planning around open ingredients saves money without making you feel as if you are eating the exact same meal repeatedly.

Frequently Asked Questions

Do I need to buy everything on this list?

No. Start with the twelve essentials and add other ingredients as you choose recipes.

A pantry should support the way you actually cook. It should not become a collection of expensive jars you never open.

Are canned beans and tomatoes good enough?

Absolutely. They are dependable, affordable shortcuts, and I use them often.

Choose plain beans and tomatoes whenever possible so you can control the salt and seasonings yourself.

Which olive oil should I use for Greek cooking?

Choose an extra-virgin olive oil that you enjoy tasting.

Store it in a cool, dark place and purchase an amount you can reasonably finish while it is still fresh.

Can I substitute dried herbs for fresh herbs?

Often, yes, but they work differently.

Add dried herbs during cooking so they have time to soften and release their flavor. Add fresh herbs near the end when you want freshness and color.

As a general starting point, use approximately one-third as much dried herb as fresh herb, then adjust to taste.

What should I make first?

For a simple and economical place to begin, try my Greek Lentil Soup.

For a comforting side dish that goes with almost everything, make my Greek Lemony Roasted Potatoes.

If you want a family-friendly main course, begin with my Greek Keftedes.

Each recipe uses ingredients you will be able to use again in many other meals.

Save the Complete Pantry Checklist

A well-stocked pantry is not about having more. It is about keeping the right ingredients close by so that a comforting meal feels possible—even on a busy day.

Start small. Cook a few recipes. Notice what your family loves, and build your pantry from there.

Before long, you will look at a bag of lentils, a can of tomatoes, or a box of orzo and see dinner instead of a group of separate ingredients.
